title: "Bounding Box"
description: "A rectangular region used to locate an object or area in an image."
term: "Bounding Box"
letter: "B"
category: "Computer Vision"
difficulty: "Beginner"
---

## Simple explanation

A bounding box is a rectangle drawn around an object or region of interest
in an image. Object-detection systems use boxes to indicate what they
found and where it appears.

## Technical explanation

A box can be represented by coordinates such as $(x_{\min}, y_{\min},
x_{\max}, y_{\max})$ or by center coordinates, width, and height. The
coordinate convention may be normalized or measured in pixels. Detection
systems predict boxes along with class scores, and evaluation commonly
compares predictions with labeled boxes using intersection over union.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Bounding boxes are a common annotation and output format in object
detection. Consistent coordinate conventions and annotation quality are
essential for training, evaluation, and integration with downstream
systems.

## How it works

An annotation tool or model specifies a rectangle using the chosen
coordinate format. To compare a prediction and a reference box, intersection
over union (IoU) is often calculated:

$$
\operatorname{IoU}(A,B) =
\frac{\operatorname{area}(A \cap B)}
{\operatorname{area}(A \cup B)}
$$

## Practical example

A traffic-camera detector can return a bounding box around each detected
vehicle along with a class label and score. A downstream tracker can use
the box coordinates to associate detections across video frames.

## Common misconceptions

- A bounding box marks an approximate rectangle, not the exact object
  outline.
- Box coordinates are meaningless without their coordinate convention and
  image dimensions.
- High overlap does not by itself establish that the object class is
  correct.
